questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on building and testing changes in a sandbox before production, even for a change that looks obviously safe?
options: Sandboxes are required by Salesforce for every change, with no exceptions enforced by the platform
Sandboxes are faster to work in than production, which is the only reason to use them
Production changes are always reverted automatically after 24 hours
A change that looks safe can still have an unanticipated side effect — like a validation rule blocking an integration's API inserts — and a sandbox is where that surprise happens to nobody real
questions.explain: The core risk isn't that changes are hard to make — it's that side effects are hard to predict. Testing in a sandbox first means the unexpected consequence surfaces somewhere that doesn't affect real users.

questions.q: In the four-stage change loop described in the lesson, what comes after moving a tested change with a Change Set?
options: Nothing further is needed — the loop ends once the change set deploys
Immediately building the next unrelated change in the same sandbox
Watching for Release Updates that might interact with the newly shipped change, and checking Setup Audit Trail / Login History afterward if anything looks off
Deleting the sandbox used to build the change
questions.explain: The loop doesn't end at deployment — watching for release updates that might interact with the change, and using the audit tools to verify if something looks wrong, are both part of the same ongoing discipline.

questions.q: What are the three questions the lesson says should be asked before every change, not after?
options: What exactly is changing and why, who else does this affect, and how would this get rolled back if it's wrong?
How much will this cost, who approved the budget, and when is the deadline?
Which profile should see this, which permission set grants it, and which role hierarchy applies?
Is this a standard object or custom object, and does it have a page layout?
questions.explain: The lesson frames change management as three concrete questions: the specific change and its reason, who besides the requester is affected, and a rollback plan decided in advance.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should an admin do if the honest answer to 'how would this get rolled back if it's wrong?' is 'I'm not sure'?
options: Deploy anyway, since rollback plans are rarely needed in practice
Treat that uncertainty as a signal to slow down before deploying, not after something breaks
Skip testing in a sandbox to save time instead
Ask a different admin to deploy it so responsibility is shared
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames 'not sure' on rollback as a reason to pause and think it through before deploying, rather than discovering the gap only after a problem occurs.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat documentation as a discipline rather than an afterthought?
options: Because Salesforce requires a documentation field to be filled in before any change can save
Because undocumented changes are automatically reverted after 90 days
Because documentation is graded as part of the Salesforce Certified Administrator exam
Because a setting changed with no note of why becomes a trap for whoever looks at it later — including a future version of the same admin who has forgotten the context
questions.explain: The lesson's point is practical, not procedural: the cost of a short documentation habit is near zero in the moment, and the payoff is real the first time someone (possibly the same admin, later) needs to understand why a setting exists.
